passages.title: Breadth or Depth in the School Curriculum?
passages.subtitle: Comparing wide high school programmes with early specialisation
paragraphs: Around the world, high schools disagree on how many subjects older teenagers should study. When designing a national curriculum, governments usually choose between two main ideas: depth or breadth. In Britain, sixteen-year-olds often drop most subjects and specialise in just three areas. By contrast, students in Ireland, Canada, and South Korea study seven or eight subjects until they finish school at eighteen.

Supporters of early specialisation say that studying fewer subjects lets teenagers build in-depth knowledge. For example, a student who wants to become a chemist or a doctor can focus full time on biology, chemistry, and mathematics. Teachers also notice that students enjoy classes more when they can drop subjects they dislike and spend energy on their favourite topics.

On the other hand, supporters of a wide timetable argue that sixteen is too young to narrow down a future career. Keeping core subjects—such as mathematics, reading, and a second language—compulsory until eighteen gives young people a well-rounded education. Today, many exciting jobs mix different fields: a video game creator needs both computer coding and visual drawing, while a green energy planner needs science and clear writing.

There is also a lively debate about history and the arts compared with STEM subjects. Because governments want strong economies, they often spend more money on computing, engineering, and physics, leaving painting, theatre, and history with fewer classroom hours. However, history teachers argue that knowing the past helps citizens make wise voting choices, while art teachers stress that creative lessons train imagination and fresh problem-solving.

To get the best of both systems, many modern schools now offer balanced diplomas like the International Baccalaureate. Students choose six subjects from science, languages, arts, and humanities—studying three at an advanced level and three at a regular level—plus an extended essay. Many parents welcome this mixed approach because it builds deep skills without closing doors too early.

passages.title: Compulsory Schooling and School Dropouts
passages.subtitle: How laws, vocational training, and adult literacy centres reduce early school leaving
paragraphs: Fifty years ago, leaving school at age 15 or 16 was completely normal because factories, farms, and shops needed plenty of young workers. Today, machines do much of that simple work, so teenagers without certificates struggle to find steady jobs. In response, countries such as England and parts of Australia have raised the legal school-leaving age to 18. Leaders hope that extra education will support social mobility, helping children from poor backgrounds move into better-paid work.

Even with stronger laws, thousands of teenagers still drop out every year. Usually, leaving school is not a sudden decision. Students show clear warning signs first, especially frequent truancy—skipping school without a good excuse—and falling test marks. Studies show that vulnerable teenagers who face family illness, unstable housing, or reading difficulties are at the highest risk of quitting early.

Dropping out creates serious problems in adulthood. Many early leavers struggle with low adult literacy, making it difficult to read rental letters, check bank bills, or follow safety signs at work. Over a lifetime, adults without basic qualifications earn much less money and are more likely to need government housing or health support.

Many teachers point out that forcing bored teenagers to sit in standard exam classes until 18 rarely solves the problem. Instead, unhappy students may cause classroom noise or simply stop turning up. Education experts say raising the age limit only works when schools create a strong vocational pathway starting at age 16. By learning practical trades such as hospitality, car mechanics, or graphic design, hands-on learners stay interested and gain real job skills.

Early care from school staff also makes a huge difference. In Norway, special support teams check attendance every week; when a student starts missing days, a youth worker visits the home to listen and solve issues like bullying or transport costs rather than fining the parents. For people who left school years ago, free adult literacy centres inside public libraries now offer friendly evening classes so anyone can build reading skills and apply for better jobs.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
passages.title: Teaching Life Skills in Schools
passages.subtitle: Should high schools teach money management, volunteering, and family care?
paragraphs: When young people graduate from high school, many can name historical kings or balance chemistry formulas, yet have no idea how to pay an electricity bill, spot an online scam, or cook simple vegetable soup. Because of this gap, parents and employers around the world are asking schools to spend more time teaching practical life skills.

Financial literacy is the skill people request most often. Today, eighteen-year-olds receive credit card adverts on their phones and can borrow money with just two clicks. Without basic money training, young adults can quickly fall into painful debt. Pilot programmes in New Zealand and Britain found that teenagers who practise making a monthly budget and comparing savings accounts handle their money much more safely after leaving school.

Another popular idea is building civic responsibility through community service. In several Canadian provinces and Japanese schools, teenagers spend time helping at animal shelters, cleaning local parks, or reading to older citizens. Supporters say these hands-on projects are powerful tools for character building, helping students develop kindness, patience, and pride in their neighbourhood far better than classroom speeches can.

Some reformers also propose teaching basic parenting skills and child care to older teenagers. They point out that caring for a baby requires knowledge about healthy food, sleep routines, and calm communication, yet almost no school covers these topics. Critics, however, argue that every culture raises children differently, so family life should be taught by parents rather than school staff.

Adding life skills to schools also brings real difficulties. Most school timetables are already packed with exam subjects, and teachers feel heavy pressure to raise reading and maths scores. Asking busy language teachers to run finance or repair workshops without extra training could lead to weak lessons. Some students also treat forced volunteering like a boring chore if they have no choice in the project.

Even with these challenges, I believe schools should not ignore everyday skills. Schools do not need to cut core subjects; instead, they can include household budgeting inside maths lessons and invite local cooks, nurses, or bank workers as guest speakers. Passing exams opens university doors, but practical life skills help young people live safely and happily once they step into the adult world.
